CHICAGO, January 25.-Hunters
who sailed forth yesterday into the
wilderness few miles from down
town Chicago to kill wolves and coy
otes came back last night empty
handed but not discouraged.


The hunters, composed of county
officials equipped with snow shoes.
rifles and camping outfit. went to the
rescue of farmers living near Chicago
who reported wolves and coyotes have
been attacking live stock and terri
flying residents.


The hunters gave UP yesterday he
cause they were unable to find fresh
tracks in the woodlands, but planned
to return to the snow-covered region
today.


The riflemen last night heard q
skeptic declare that the wolves and

Nan Hartley posed for living. She
hadn't any particular talent, ana mel
beauty was such a decided asset that
at the suggestion of a friend she hao
commercialzed it.


Nan was very beautiful. She had
tiny face that looked as If it had been
carved out OF a cameo. Her nose was
small and her lovely, wide mouth
curved over perfect teeth. Her eyes
were blue-violet blue-and her dark
ahair, short, of course, waved back
from a broad, white forehead. She
had the kind of beauty that artists
went mad over, so that she seldom
had any trouble getting work.


She posed for magazine covers. H.
Illustrations of different kinds, com
mercial art and anything she could
get.


1t wasn't easy work, because 1t
meant holding a pose that was often
very difficult. Sometimes the artist
would forget, too. Absorbed in his
work. he would neglect TO say:


Don't you want to rest, Miss Hart
ley?"


Nan could never bear to interrupt
an artist, so she would grit her teeth
and hold on for dear life. Sometimes,
when she at last relaxed, her tortured
muscles would ache like a toothache.
once when she had been crouching on
the floor in an unnatural pose she had
toppled over, and the sudden, sharp
agony OF relaxation had made her
burst into hysterical tears.


A long list of artists had her name
and address, and would call her on the
telephone when they needed her type.
She averaged about $40 a week, al
though there were weeks when she
made more.


Nan had gone into the work of pos
ing with some dread. She had read
magazine stories about the things
that went on in artists studios, and
had formed her ideas accordingly. She
had visions of tiger-skin rugs hanging
from balconies and of the artists
themselves working in velvet dressing
gowns and trying to make love to
her.


She had started out in fear and
trembling, going from studio to studio;
but, for the most part, she had found
her fears groundless. OF course, she
had had one or two unpleasant expert
ances, but she might have had those
In any business Office.


In almost every case the artist, usu-
ally in a smock or a WORKOUT dress.
ing gown, worked in a big. bare
studio. Canvasses Uttered the walls
They were piled everywhere. The
harsh, searching light from huge
north skylight filled the room.


The same formula was repeated
again and again.


Nan would say, shyly: 81 am look.
ing for work"


And the artist, usually in the midst
of some creative work, and, for that
reason, busy and distracted, would
stop because of her amazing beauty.
At first she was embarra ssed at the
way they stared at her; but later she
realized that there was nothing per
sonal about it.


They stared at her critically be-
cause her features were so fiawless
Already they were fitting her into
some possible creation.


They all said the same thing, too:

Maine lakes have certain common
aracteristics-deeply wooded banks.
hilly surroundings, clear water. reedy
coves-so that you could say OF such
bodies of water anywhere that they
are like Maine lake." But there
are great differences between the in
dividual lakes. Big Sabago, shaped
exactly like a fat turnip, has COM
paratively low shores; it is broad,
fine piece of water, and that is about
all one can say of it. But only few
miles away lies Long Lake, 10 miles
long. scarcely q mile wide at any
point, almost as straight as a ramrod.
with the hills looking down on it. All
through the game region there are
many of these same longitudinal lakes,
occupying what seems once to have
been riffs or cracks in the landscape
and generally in connected chains.
Every one of them has its especial
beauty. There are reedy. lonely ponds
where the loon laughs and lunges.
and there are lakes like Bear Pond,
in Turner and Hartford, which is
wholly surrounded with sandy beaches.
and where the children wade and
splash in sparkling water for long
distance without danger and are
always within reach of their ice
cream cones. And everywhere noble
chains of lakes. like the great and
famous ones in the north, or like the
Belgrade and Winthrop Lakes. and
the chain that comes down from Til.
ton Pond through David, Parker,
Crotched, Lovejoy. Pocasset and And.
roscoggin lakes. which last discharges
through Deer River into the Andros-
coggin River. From each of these
lakes there is drop of Is to 19 feet
creating a water power which is in
nearly every instance availed Of for
some light manufacturing purpose.

plans and obtained a promise of full
support for her transatlantic flight.

half for an airplane and the remainder
for making exhibition flights around
Germany

Rasche one of the cleverest and surest
pilots in the world. She is the only
woman in Germany possessing an air.
plane. She learned flying from the

By the Associated Press.


NEW YORK, June 14.--Yale will
rule favorite to retain the inter.
collegiate polo championship when
the annual tournament opens Thurs
day on the grounds of the Westminster
Biltmore Country Club at Rye, N. Y.
Five teams are entered.


Yale is rated highly on account of
the Blues showing indoors and vic.
tories outdoors over Pennsylvania
Military College and Princeton. Be
sides the teams of those institutions,
West Point and Harvard tours will
seek the title.


For the first time the tourney will
be round robin with each team
meeting each of the others and the
winner the combination taking the
most games. The final is set for June
25. The college tournament is the
first major engagement of a polo
season which will bring at its close
the ninth international duel between
the United States and Great Britain.

ANNAPOLIS, February "a re-
markable program of sports at the
Naval Academy Saturday will In
clude contests with Syracuse in three
lines OF sport, swimming, water
polo and fencing. There will be
three other varsity events and three
for the Plebes.


Syracuse and the Navy are two
of the four unbeaten teams in the
intercollegiate Swimming Associa-
ton. Yale and Princeton being the
others. Neither has lost a swimming
or water polo match.


Navy has shown much strength in
water polo this year and should win
in that sport, but the Syracuse swim
ming team, which has already beaten
Pennsylvania, should give the Mid
shipmen much trouble, and the result
is by no means a certainty.

man in Mergott that the Navy has,

crack middle distance man.


The outstanding wrestling match
of the season is expected when the
Navy team meets the grapplers of
Oklahoma Agricultural and Mechan-
ical College. This team has been
champion OF the Missouri Valley Con-
ference for years and has not lost
a match since 1920. Most of its mem
bers have never lost a match.


The team includes three national
champions: De Marsh. 115 pounds;
Patterson, 125 pounds, and Strack,
unlimited weight class. The latter
was also a member of the last
Olympic team and the runner-up

afternoon is a basket ballgame against
Gettysburg College. while the Plebes
stage thes contests: Basket ball,

ington; fencing, Forest Park School,

By the Associated freSS.


BIRMINGHAM. England. May 21.-
Old English villages in agricultural
sections vary in age from 1000 to
]. 500 years, and bits of their history
are often written in quaint signs
which have survived for many centu-
ries.
Next to the churches, the inns and
smithies are usually the oldest build
ings in the villages which have not
been ingulfed by industries. Before
the days of railways and motors the
smithv was the center to which every
one had to go in peace and in war.
Inn signs are particularly useful in
tracing the history of villages. as they
often show the seals or insignia OIL
lords under whose protection the VII
lage thrived in past ages and fire.
quently indicate the past character OF
the neighborhoods.


But the purely fanciful signs are
even more interesting than those
which have historical background.
One sign which used to be very COM
mon on old English inns was the
Five Ais" The sign represents the
King, "who governs all'': the bishop,


who prays for all'; the lawyer, who
pleads for all"; the soldier, ''who
fights for ALL" and the laborer. who
works for all"


The Lord of Mischief" sign, which
is less common. shows man carrying
woman on his back.


Although 80 individuals, and some
times fewer, in direct line of descent
link the present villagers with their
ancestors before the Norman con-
quest, the villagers of today often
know little about the histories Of their
communities, and search Of village
records often yields little information
about the early struggles Of the tiny
communities which are made up of
low brown cottages screened by trees
and vines.

The worlds nest-building cham
pions have been discovered at the
Zoo.


They are a pair of African
weaver birds, brilliantly colored
creatures about the size Of English
sparrows. Yesterday the small bird
cage was opened for the first time
this Spring and the occupants al
lowed to fly into the outdoor cage.
in the center of which a hemlock
tree had been planted.


Ordinarily they are out weeks
earlier. They will not build nests
until they are outside. Consequent
ly their Spring schedule has been
delayed badly this year.


AS soon as they got into the sun
shine the two weavers began pluck
ing hemlock twigs and carrying
them inside, where they built their
nest on one of the supporting poles
of the cage.


The weaver nest Is a masterpiece
Of pathological architecture. The
twigs are woven into a tight wall.
The nest is rooted and has a side
entrance. In less than two hours
the birds had their nest completed
before any of the other small
birds who started their home-b build

Mackaye, actress, today faced trial
for attempting to conceal facts sur
rounding the recent death of her hus-
band, Ray Raymond. musical comedy
star, who died after fist fight with
Paul Kelly, film actor.


Miss Mackaye, for whose love Ray
mond and Kelly admittedly fought,
was indicted as an accessory after the
fact and for compromising a felony
in withholding information regarding
the fist fight when the death was re-
ported.


DIR. Walter J. Sullivan, physician,
who attended Raymond, was indicted
with Miss Mackaye, but has been
granted a separate trial.


Kelly was found guilty of man
slaughter and is under a to 10 years
sentence.


Will Call Same Witnesses.


Deputy District Attorney Forrest
Murray, who prosecuted Kelly, ad-
mitted that due to the nature of the
State must prove all over again that
homicide had been committed and that
her admitted lover was the guilty
party.


Seldom, if ever, has such an unusual
situation arisen in a Los Angeles
courtroom, the prosecutor said. He
confirmed the belief that virtually
every witness who testified at Kelly's
trial has been called to appear against
Miss Maskaye. The State contended
and introduced evidence to prove that
the love affair of Kelly and Miss Mack
aye caused Raymond to order the
young film actor from his home, and
later to provoke the fist attack from
which Raymond died.


Assume Double Role.


Attorneys Roger Marchetti and Jer.
ny Geisler, who will defend Miss Mack
aye, will assume the role of defend
ers of Kelly also. They said they
would make new and different at
tempt to establish that Raymond died
of natural causes and not from the
effects of the fight as the State con-
tended.


The trial was scheduled to begin late
today.

BOSTON. July 10 OP.-The volun-

Sacco and Bartolomeo VanZetti today
entered its third day with State
prison officials still inclined to attrib-
ute their fast to hot weather rather
than to admit the condemned men
were actually on hunger strike.


Vanzetti continues to sip coffee and
to refuse other food, while Sacco has
declined everything. Both men, how
ever, have running water in their
cells.


DR.. Edmund V. Wilson, assistant
superintendent of the City Hospital,
said that if the men drink no water
they could not live longer than 10
days. Their seven years imprison-
ment since their arrest in 1920 for
the Staying of a paymaster and guard,
and their continued Incarceration
throughout the fight which has been
waged to overturn the verdict of the
trial jury, has greatly weakened
them, he believed.


Former Fast Broken.


The question of forcible feeding has
not yet been considered by Warden
Hendry. but he has been given full
authority by Sanford Bates, State
commissioner of corrections, to deal
with any situation that may arise.


In 1928. while awaiting disposition
of motions for new trial, Sacco con.
Quoted a hunger strike for more than
a month. but desisted after being
forcibly fed.


Gov. Alvan T. Fuller and his spe.
clal advisory committee are pushing
their review of the celebrated case.


The committee had before it today
a request from William G. Thompson,
counsel for defense, for complete
stenographic copy Of all testimony it
had heard.


Sacco and Vanzetti exhausted their
last recourse to the State courts when
the Supreme Court recently refused
their latest petition for retrial, and
hope now rests in Gov. Fuller and
his counsel. Execution, originally
set for the week of July 10, has been
postponed by the governor until the
week of August 10.

mer dress. She was also presented

ture sweets, revolving lanterns, gold
and silver fans, toy bird cage and
numerous other costly gifts.


Miss America will be viewed by the
public at the Educational Museum in
Ueno Park.

Of Japan are preparing handsome
Japanese dolls for presentation to
American children some time next
Spring. Some of these dolls have al

That was the story of my little
tree That was the story Of all
life, all love, all birth and death
it was written plain for me to
read-in those few leaves-in
that small pot of soil.


What tales of conquest that
brown earth could tell! The salty
ebb and flow of the first sea, with
the thin line of life left by reced-
ing waves. The dead and crum-
pied crust of that spent life was
in that soil. But not the force
that made it live-that force
went on.


Huge lizards fighting for their
food in Mesozoic swamps. Their
blood soaked in the soil but not
their force-that force went on.


The first small mammal lnuddled
in its hairy coat. while the great
Ice Cap blotIed out all other life
on earth. Its saving coat had
gone back to the soil but not its
force-that force went on.


And then those first bent men,
with long arms fumbling like
hairy apes and small eyes peering
from their low-browed skulls.
Long. long ago their bones had
turned to dust but not their force
or dreams they still went on.


THEIR FORCE WENT ON!


That inner fire. that urge and
thrust and prayer which we name
Soul. or God or fail to name at
all--that fire did not die. It could
not pass awav. 1t shed and shed
again its transient house. The
scales and fangs and claws, the lit.
tie appetites and brief. bright days
OF fame, were dust upon the high
way OF the years. But that bright
flame which warmed them did not
die.


They might e drowned in water.
burned In fire. wasted by sick
ness. hanged upon cross. but
still their Force stayed victor over
Life and Death.


Force could not be imprisoned
In a tomb.


Each tiny seeding burst from
out the grave.


Each bird at Matching broke
from some white cell.


Each babe at borning won the
fight once more.


There, all about me, stood the
shining proof. Not Just on Easter
morning but on every day. need
not wait till Easter for a miracle.
Each second saw Force conquer
over Death.


And all my garden glowed with
Victory!

TOXIC, April 12.--Forged with
ceremonial solemnity, the new state
sword of Emperor Hirohito is in the
hands of the most famous craftsmen
in Japan. When the new mikado
goes to join his fathers, the weapon
will be lowered into the imperial
sarcophagus with his body.

the customs of his father, the late
Emperor Yoshihito, and his grand
father Emperor Meiji. who used
only swords made many years ago
by noted artisans.


Sadakatsu Tsukiyama of Osaka,
the most noted modern swordmaker
of Japan, started the forging with
prayers and ceremony. Priests
streWed incense and Tsukiyama, with
two assistants, all in white ceremonial
garments, solemnly placed the iron
ore in The furnace and a new sceptre
for q new mikado was begun.

ness of Tsukiyama. the weapon will
be turned over to Riko Hishida, the
leading sword polisher, who will give
it the finishing touches.

That's the point hosts of my readers
have reached-the very end OF every
thing.


They arrived at this desolate spot
along the roads of Heartbreak and
Disappointment. And, having reached
the very limits of their endurance,
they sit down at the crossways and
wall aloud.


Very bad policy. Now's the very
time when they should have their eyes
wide open for a new road-a road
leading away from the end of every
thing and beginning something all
over again.


It's when a girl finds herself at the
very bottom OF the black pit Of despair
that she can most confidently look
forward to an unexpected means of
exit from the unpleasant situation.


But there's hardly damsel alive
who is inclined to believe me. And
because they don't believe me they sit
and wall and keep their eyes tight
shuk. so that they can't possibly find
any opportunity for escape from their
dismal frame of mind.


You take a dame like Janet, who
had all the earmarks of a nice, intelli-
gent kid until Rodney, the boy won
der. threw her over for buxom girl
from Texas.


Then Janet proceeded to revert to
the primitive. She tore out handfuls
OF hair. she gnashed her teeth, she
behaved like any good cave lady, and
then she subsidized with heart-rending
shrek as her Rodney bore the trium-
phant Texas lady to the altar.


On the day of the wedding and re.
ception she knew she had arrived at
the end of everything. There was
nothing more for her to live for. She
had nothing to keep her alive.


She sat mute and cold through the
ceremony. She went to the reception
with her head held high, but her heart
breaking. She didn't let Rodney see
how she was suffering. In fact, she
was so busy conCealing her hurt from
him that she hadn't time for anything
else.


1t never occurred to her to pay
attention to the tall. dark boy who
had come up from Texas for the fes-
tivities. She just didn't see him. She
hadn't the faintest suspicion that he
liked her. Even when he made it
known. shyly, she could barely hear
him. All her thoughts were centered
on Rodney, and the tall. dark boy was
a shadowy figure who didn't matter.


lie StuCk AROUND lOT Il IndtleT ol

all the time his worth and devotion
were lost on Janet. who dreamed of
Rodney, thought of him, cried about
him.


Then miracle happened. Rodney
landed in town. He came alone. He
and the wife had not hit it off. Rod.
ney was a divorced man. Janet
thrilled at the news.


Without even glancing inNthe direc-

Everybody had always known Rod

wise license. 1t sought to have this

During an uprising of the Zulus

stick.

lutely certain.

sourceful colonel tried bluff. Assum.
ing a determined expression, he point.
ed his walking stick straight at the

strange weapon AS they walked back,

walking stick.

familiar thing to the Zulu. They


also were wildcats with knives. and.
although they had never handled guns,

strange, long stick which the white
man menaced them with was some
! thing quite new to them.
| Suddenly the colonel, still walking

shoulder, like gun. With one accord

went

ago, has not been heard from, and,
as she carried radio equipment, 1t is
feared she may have been damaged in
the storm.


The Mexican steamer Bolivar, which
left Salina Cruz, Mexico, August %.
and was due here a week ago, also
has not been heard from and fears
are felt for her safety.


The freighter Horace X Baxter of
San Francisco last night was re-
ported hard aground on an island near

appeared in little danger.

painters were. preparing the
Cunard liner Mauretania for her
departure they found a pigeons
nest containing a single egg built
in the curve of the gigantic
anchor. The nest had been built
and an egg laid since the ships
arrival week ago.


The nest. made of bits Of string
and wood and even tiny pieces Of
wire, was removed to a safer place,
but the pigeon, whose home it
was, would not approach it after
it had been disturbed. The bird
fled frantically about the anchor
but would not alight on the deck
where the nest had been placed.

SEATTLE, Wash, December 20
To foil the devils which Japanese sea-
faring men were convinced brought
her misfortune the death ship" Ryo
Yei Maru, has been consigned to the
flames.


The vessel a fishing smack, drifted
on the broad Pacific eleven months
while her crew of y Nipponese fisher
men sickened, starved and died.


The Ryo Yei, valued at about
1900. was secretly lowed to an iso-
lated beach on Puget Sound Sunday.
her hold filed with waste and soaked
with oil, set afire and reduced to
mass of smoldering ashes and twisted
metal.


It had been planned to ship the
Ryo Vel back to Japan, and arrange
ments were made to place the 85-foot
boat on the after deck of an American
mail liner for the return voyage, but
the plans were Cancelled when it was
learned that the families of the un-
fortunate fishermen did not want her
returned.


The fisher folk of Misaki, Japan,
where the ship was built, were con-
WINGED that EVIL spirits had taken pos
session of the ship and her return to
Japan might bring other calanities.


No part of the Inflated ship was
saved lest a demon escape the fire.


The Ryo Yei was sighted off the
Washington coast October 81. She
had set sail on a fishing trip from
Japan December 5, 1926 The last
survivors of the crew died in MAY,
1927, diary found aboard the vessel
revealed.

CHICAGO. November 10.-Announce-

today to ease the wheat market here.

gradually warming, the first samples
of the newly cut wheat being OF good
quality. Starting unchanged to as off,
Chicago wheat later showed sag all
around. Corn and oats were likewise
easy, corn opening unchanged to II
down and later declining little more.
Provisions underwent a material set
back.


Word from Argentina that the first
cutting of wheat this season had taken
place in the extreme northern part of
the country and that harvest condi-
tions were favorable was given bear
ish emphasis today by news that
Liverpool quotations were responsible
for the fact that latest figures on the
worlds available supply are larger

were current that the official estimate
tomorrow of the 1927 Canadian wheat
yield would show a decided increase
and there was talk. too. that greater
amount of acreage than usual has
been prepared for next years Canadian
crop.

started easy. sympathizing with wheat.
unfavorable weather led later to up

ington was due after the close today

accounts and to hold fresh speculative

By the Associated Press.


The United States Government has
Just paraded so equine aristocrats be-
fore the admiring gaze of the Nation.


All of the animals were Morgans--
alert, powerful specimens of horse
flesh, poised to perfection. The exhi.
bition was held on the United States
Morgan Horse Farm at Middlebury,
vt. New Englanders predominated
in the groups of spectators.


The breed, until a few years ago
virtually extinct, originated in New
England. 1t was established by
stallion, Justin Morgan, foaled in 1893
and named after is owner, school
teacher who lived near Rudolph, VT.
Chosen as the founder of race. JUS
tin Morgan outwalked, outpulled and
outran all Of the other horses IN his
section of the country.


Known Many Years.


For many years the breed -four
ished. Morgans were used almost TO
the exclusion of other general utility
horses in the New England States.
The first break came with popular de-
sire for trotting speed. which resulted
in a mixture of Morgan and thorough
bred stock.


When the Civil War came and the
lst Vermont Cavalry dashed into ac-
ton, the troopers sabers flashed from
the backs of steelmuscled MOrgans.
Gen. Sheridan mounted Morgan on
his famous ride from Winchester.
Later the horse was named Ninches-
ter. His hide. stuffed and mounted, 10
preserved at the National Museum.


The first public effort to preserve
the disappearing Morgan strain was
made in 1906 when the United states
Department of Agriculture and the
Vermont State Experiment station
wore authorized to assemble a small
band of Morgan mares at the station
farm near Burlington.


Government Farm Started.
The government farm, approximate
ing 900 acres, was started When the
late Col Joseph Battell of Middlebury.
VT, founder of the American Morgan
| Register, gave the Department OF Ag'
riculture a 400-acre farm at Wey-
| bridge. Stock for the farm has been
obtained from Morgan blood in Ken
tuckv Kansas. Texas. New York,
| Washington, Iowa, Rhode Island, New
Hampshire, Illinois and the native Ver-
mont.


At the outbreak of the World war
foreign agents came to America lot
cavalry horses. There were not
enough Morgans.


Even the United States Cavalry
was handicapped. The situation led to
development of the present Cavalry
Remount Service, which sends 800
stations throughout the country Tor
the breeding of suitable steeds should
there be another demand. or that
number 81 are Morgans, centered
principally at Kansas City, Mo.
Inquiries Received.
The Government has received in
ouiries for Morgans from the Prov
inces Of Quebec, Ontario and Alberta,
Canada, and from Cuba, Porto Rico.
Central America, South America, Ja-
pan and China, as well as from every
section of the United States.


New York City's mounted ponce
win prizes with Morgans; cattlemen
say they have the intelligence ana
courage to "hold'' steer after II
has been roped; polo players like tneir
quick wit and hardness; saddle dev-
otees prefer their smart, alert walk
easy trot and collected canter; farm-
ers take pride in their short, strong
legs and round, full-muscled bodies.

All the homage a nation paid to its

Lillian Gish, emotional star of
many fine photoplays, will be the
picture star at Loew's Columbia this
week, beginning this afternoon, in her
newest romantic drama, The Scarlet
Letter" from the Nathaniel Haw
thorne classic, at it's Washington
premiere.


Victor Seastrom, Scandinavian di-
rector of HE Who Gets Slapped"
produced 1.-THE Scarlet Letter" for
Metro Goldwyn Mayer release. The
cast includes also Lars Hanson. the
Barrymore of Sweden who makes
his American debut in this picture;
Henry B. Walthall, who was fea-
tured with Miss Gish in Birth of a
Nation" and Karl Dane, the famous
Slim of THE Big Parade"


THE Scarlet Letter" is a romance
of Puritan New England, in which
Miss Gish impersonates Hester
Prynne, the New England Puritan
seamstress, whose gay light-hearted-
ness brings her under the discipline and
romantic interest of the young Puri-
tan pastor. Dimesdale. From Testers
short confinement in the stocks springs
a romance of almost tragic intensity.


The picture, with New England
settings and costumes, depicts the
morals and manners of Puritan New
England in the early part of the
seventeenth century. The Columbia
Symphony Orchestra, under Leon
Brusilof, will provide an appropriate
overture and atmospheric accompani-
ment. The Pathe newsreel, Topics of
the Day and other features will lend
variety to the program.

after some watching-With none of
the modest grace and speed of the
true sensitive plant of the Old World
tropics.


All the sensitive plants. cassias,
mimosas and the like, are being
studied by plant Psychologists, and
one can hardly pick up a botanical
journal these days without reading a
bit of sharp controversy.


A Hindu botanist. Sir Jagadir Bose.

consequently feelings Further, they
have hearts, according to the learn
ed Indian. And he has photographs.
even autographs" of plants to prove
that they react almost humanity to
stimuli and injury Perhaps it is
only chance that the Hindu philos-
ophy perceives an animism in all
things and that the botanist finds
plants human. But YOU can imagine
what sarcastic remarks western
science makes.


All the while, under the July sun,
in the golden glare of Summer sun
light. the little sensitive pea blooms.
opens and shuts its ferny leaves and
delights the simple at heart. who
know not nor care how the plant
performs this shy miracle.

PEKING, April 21.-American Ma
rines today scaled a wall of the
Soviet embassy compound and forced
the gate. after which guards of the
other powers entered


Guards Of the protocol powers took
over control of the western wall Of
the compound The move was de-
scribed as necessary for carrying out
the regular defense program of the
legation quarter.


The Chinese authorities agreed to
the step, but owing to hitch the
gates were locked.


A few Chinese police are still oc-
cupying the premises recently raided,
but they are expected to leave soon.
when the Soviet compound viii be
vacant except for the foreign guards
along the wall. Soviet consular otfi-
cials still occupy the embassy proper.


Soviet Demands Refused.


The Peking government dispatched
instructions to it's representative in
Moscow today to inform the Soviet
government that a careful eXamina-
ton was still being made of the docu-
ments seized in the raid on Soviet
buildings in the embassy compound
at Peking two weeks ago, and that
consequently the government has no
way of complying with the Soviet
demands in connection with the raid.


The Chinese representative was told
to inform the Soviet that the raid
was conducted on premises outside
the embassy proper, which the police
serupulously refrained from entering.


Illegal Practices Alleged.


"True," the reply states, diplomats
enjoy special immunities, but that
does not confer on them the right to
carry out illegal practices. Even a
casual preliminary examination re-
vealed arms, while the seized docu-
ments disclosed much discriminating
evidence, such as communistic propa-
ganda and an extensive secret cor
respondence with places throughout

ley ID. Butler. comma nder of the Amer
lean Marines in China; Rear Admiral
Blakely. commanding the Sd Light
Cruiser Division. and Brig. Gen. Cast
ner, commander of the Tientsin gar
rison of the 18th American Infantry.
arrive! in Peking today for confer
ence with American diplomatic Off
cials and commanders of the legation
guard regarding preca utionary defense
measures. They will return to Tien-
tsin tomorrow. when Gen. Duncan,
commander of the British Shanghai
defense force, is due to arrive.


Investigations upon the spot by
American and British generals and
consultations with French Japanese
and Italian military authorities prop
ably will determine what further for
eign forces shall be dispatched to
northern China.


Marines to Arrive Tonight.


The transport Henderson. with 500
American Marines aboard. is expect.
ed off Tientsin tonight. The arrival
of further British French and pos
sibly Japanese forces has had a re-
assuring effect on the foreign commu-
mites of Peking and Tientsin, although
numerous women and children and
much personal property have been sent
to Tientsin and seaside resorts in the
last few days.


This was due principally to official
notification from the British strongly
advising evacuation of women and
children according to plans formulated
last April, when the situation seemed
worse and the Nanking outraGes were
still fresh. Other legations have not
issued similar advice.


Lull Occurs i'm Warfare.


The lull in the North China war;
fare also has eased the tension of the
Fengtien forces, which are consolidat-
ing the defense lines of northern
HOnan and western Chihli. They nc

forces further collapse along the

turn public attention to the PROC

same level. The problem has been met

which we used to call the rural dis
tricts." Many country roads now carry

carried when the Embarrassing dan
ger first came under discussion. Some
much used rail- and wagon road cross.

work.

over railroad tracks and live, but
fatal mistakes are made every day
and the auto.road; and railroad grade
crossing is a danger that must sooner
or later be removed. Traffic on auto
mobile roads is growing and.n0 doubt
will grow for an indefinite time. One
great peril in any community is the
grade crossing and every community
should exert itself to have that dan
ger removed.


Washington will take to itself the
warming Of this tragedy.

small bergs in the Strait of Belle Isle,

merged lodge of a big berg and
canted steeply. It had been foggy for

sequently was proceeding slowly, with
q keen lookout. But the tall iceberg
appeared to rise suddenly out of the
mist.


1t was $50 in the afternoon and
many of the passengers were on deck.
Others hurried up, feeling the shock.
They We're ordered to don lifebelts.
Lifeboats were swung out and crews
stood ready to launch them.


In the meantime the Montcalm
righted herself and slid off the ledge.
An examination showed that a pro-
peller blade was gone. but otherwise
only the paint was Scraped.


The fog continued for two days and
the ship was unable to proceed. Other
vessels We're similarly held up and
sirens were heard on all sides.


Eventually the fog lifted and the
Montcalm, although somewhat Grip
pied. was able to proceed at reduced
speed.

DEAD MANS FLAT. Ariz.. Apri
13.-In the basin of the Little Colo
RADIO River, a short distance north oi
The Wupatki ruins. once the home oi
the prehistoric Hopi Indians, whose
descendants people the villages north
east Of here, Mrs. Helena May Smith
Of Chautauqua County. New York, is
making what she calls mosaic rock
pictures from fine sands screened
through silk


The studio she has established lies
in the most rugged and desolate part
of northern Arizona in the shadow of
the snow-crowned San Francisco
peaks. The valley of the Little Colo
RADIO is notable for the variety Of its
coloring in this vicinity. and most of
the vivid hues are caused by vari-
Colored stones and pebbles


Yield Hundred Shades.


Mrs. Smith and her husband, Jo-
seph Il. Smith, a musician. discovered
about two years ago that the stones
and pebbles could be pulverized to
Weld more than a hundred shades of
fine sand. Experiment with the sands
and wet concrete led to the production
Of the rock pictures.


Mrs. Smith is a trained artist, hav-
ing painted with oil colors on canvas
for many years. She discovered that
she could apply the sands TO a base of
wet concrete to achieve a picture
which had the general appearance of
tapestry. The first mosaic rock pic
ture, a landscape, was finished some
six months ago.


Can Duplicate Oil.


Her productions since include still
life. marines. animal and desert scenes
wherein pale moons cast silvery
lights on yellow beaches and white
capped surf, storm clouds roll across
blue skies and sinking coyotes add
touch OF life to the barren, brown
hills of Arizona.


To the vari-colored sands Mrs.
Smith has added copper, silver and
lead ores. She has investigated sands
from the Painted Desert. but finds
them useless to her, as they are most
" volcanic ash, too soft for her pur-
pose.


ANY picture made with oils can
be reproduced just as accurately with
colored sands Mrs. Smith maintains.

north of Mexico City.

and Hortensia, were among those who

PARIS, November 10.-Regular air
mail service between France and
South America will be undertaken
next year.


Financial support for the project
was assured yesterday when the
finance committee of the Chamber OF
Deputies voted 100000 francs as a
subvention to the Latecoere company.
which for some time past has ex-
plotted the air mail line between
France and Africa.


After the recent successful flight OF
Dieudonne Costes and Joseph LIE Brix
from Paris to Buenos Aires in six
hops, one of them across the South
Atlantic without stopping, this COM
pany obtained a contract with the
Argentine government for handling
transatlantic air mail. The Chilean
government also contracted for
combination air mail service with the
posts delivered to Chile from Argen.
tina by rail.


Although the planes will follow the
same route as the pathfinders, Costes
and LIE Brix, there will be no attempt
at first to span the Atlantic regularly
in one hop. The service will be con-
Quoted partly by airplane and partly
by steamship. full advantage being
taken of the islands along the route.

attention than their more colorful
cousins.


+ Research work now being con-
Quoted along the Texas border may
prove that the desert plants have
commercial value. Experiments are

of the biology department of Sui Ross
State Teachers College, and Capt. G..
D. Wood of Alpine.


Hundreds of varieties of plants,
ferns, shrubs. cact and So grasses
now grow along the Mexican border,
and nearly a score have shown traces
of properties having commercial
value.


Produce Rubber and Wax.


Already rubber and wax are being
produced in commercial quantities
from plants found in Brewster County.
Soap, glue and fibers are possibilities
from others when properly handled
and utilized, the experts say, and the
investigation is just beginning.


Up TO this time, only two indus
tries have been developed from the
great number and variety of native
plants Astounding in the Big Bend
country. From the candelilla plant
q high grade of wax is extracted and
sent to New York and foreign coun-
tries, and the guayule shrub is yield
ing crude rubber, which is being
used for many rubber products.





Other Rubber Producers.


In addition to the guayule plant.
another shrub produces rubber. 1t is
the mariola, sometimes called the
male guayule plant. Both of these
Tubber,producing plants resemble to
the inexperienced eye the gray sage
brush. The guayule produces about
II per cent rubber, while the mariola
yields only about ? per cent.


The candelilla plant is a perennial
shrub in which tube-like roots shoot
up hundreds of stems somewhat
smaller than lead pencil in diameter
and from 1 to feet in height


Experiments are being conducted
with the yucca plants, which contain
a substance which removes dirt from
hair and wooden goods; the Spanish
dagger, which has fiber which can
be used, and with the ocotilla, or gum
plant.

business of the mining companies.

Mine Workers were engaged in an un-
lawful conspiracy to prevent the in
terstate shipment Of non-union coal.

BY the Associated Press.


CHICAGO, September 3.-The APP
partition of movieless Sunday in
Chicago wavered uncertainty today as
theater owners and their locked out
union operators discussed negotiations
toward an agreement to reopen the
shows


Representatives of the two groups
spent most of the night in making the
first step toward affecting a recon
ciliation-an arbitration conference.
Although the session ended at 4
am. without any agreement reached,
both sides made known that overtures
had been made indicating a settlement
might be brought about before to-
morrow.


Charles C. Pettijohn. general coun-
sci for the Motion Picture Producers
and Distributors of America, said that
although no statement could be made
regarding the night conference, both
sides had commenced getting together
for an agreement"


May Agree Today.


1.-THE session ended at about 4
O'clock" Mr.. Pettijohn said, and the
men went home to get some sleep,
but before the day is over they prob
ably will come together again and
reach some definite agreement. Both
parties will be available at any time. y


The conference was attended by
John Balaban and Asher Levy, repre-
senting the exhibitors, and Thomas j.
Reynolds and Thomas Maloy, repre-
senting the unions.


Both groups had remained dead
locked throughout the week since the
theaters were closed Monday, and had
declared they would not arbitrate.


Mayor William Hale Thompson
voluntarily stepped into the breach
late yesterday and got the parties to-
gether for a conference.


Other Cities Involved.


The city has been virtually without
movies since last Monday, only few
theaters remaining open
after the lockout was declared.


Theater disputes in other parts or
the country also were entering new
stages. In Sedalia, Mo-, the operators
and stage hands of two leading
theaters won their strike when the
owners acceded to demands for per
cent wage increase.


At the same time, another strike
of operators and stage hands threat
ened in Cleveland, where the unions
they would declare walk
out in one week unless their demands
for a II per cent wage increase were
needed. They also are seeking new
working conditions. Seven hundred
men were involved.


In Decatur, Ill.,, differences be-
tween the theaters and their union
employees were settled with the excep-
ton of a dispute between two of the
houses and their union musicians who
sought to add to the orchestras.

equality in the Superior Normal

Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK, April 29.-The stock
market today pursued the normal
course after q violent reaction. There
was heavy selling at the start, with
further declines in active issues, then
short covering set in and there was
a brisk recovery. In general, stocks
showed more resistance to efforts to
depress quotations and here and there
throughout the list there were in
stances of renewed operations for the
advance.


The oils were still in disfavor. One
of the noteworthy features was the
failure of these stocks to show rally
ing power. Notwithstanding their pro-
longed decline. For instance, there
was a spread between the high and
low for 1927 in Marland of 221a points,
or approximately 3S per cent. So
sweeping a loss would in itself ordi-
narily bring about some upward re-
action, and the fact that this did not
appear is a fair measure of the pessi-
mistic attitude Wall Street still pre-
serves toward the oils.


Shell Union Low.


The new lows in this part Of the
list included Shell Union and Barns
dali. The last named was especially
heavily sold, ignoring entirely the
comparatively good showing in the
first quarter report. BarnSdall COW
cred dividend requirements with a
good margin, in contrast with many
other more popular oil stocks.


Railroad shares did better as a rule
Chicago Great Western, preferred and
common, stood out prominently as va
rious stories were passed around con-
corning buying for control. At least
three larger systems were mentioned
as desirous of anneXing Chicago Great
Western. Bangor & Aroostook con-
tinued Its meteoric career, opening at
new high since the stock was listed
and then going through a bewildering
series Of wide fluctuations. The Mis-
souri, Pacific shares were sold for a
while on f1ood-damage reports, but
later came back somewhat. The same
was true of Rock Island, which was
helped by the highly favorable March
earnings statement.


Standard Investment shares, such
as New York Central and Atchison
among the rails, United States Steel
and General Motors among the indus
trials and utilities of the grade of
Brooklyn Union Gas and American
Water Works, all enjoyed good recov-
cries from the lows of the day before.
The last named went to a new 1927
high. General Motors, after dipping
TO 1854, rallied over three points.
United States Steel acted in much the
same fashion, although the range was
not so great.


Hudson & Manhattan Up.
Special buying appeared in Hudson
Manhattan, putting that stock up
to the best Of the year. There was no
explanation for the interest, and the
story about the Pennsylvania taking
over the property has been repeatedly
denied. Pennsylvania, incidentally,
was better supported, both Thursday
and today, than almost any other of
the railroad stocks of its class. Baiti-
more & Ohio and Reading were two
others in which the confident buying
was in progress.


Weak spots included some of the
rubber shares. United States Rubber
was pressed for sale early in the day,

year. The predicted advance in tire
prices is relied upon to stimulate the

With the Arkansas River receding
from Fort Smith south, a new flood
threat was developed along the
White and Black Rivers today, as
both streams were reported rising
rapidly near their headwaters, as a
result of heavy rains through southern
Missouri and north Kansas yesterday


The rise along the White and the
Black, which empties into the former
stream. will not affect the upper
Arkansas. but will add to it's volume
near the Mississippi. A fall of 8 OF
a foot was registered here yesterday
and H. s. Cole, Government meteor.
ologist here, said the river would con-
tinue to recece for several days. Heavy
rains in Kansas late last week have
caused the Arkansas to rise in it's
upper reaches, but before the new rise
reaches here, the river will have re-
ceded greatly.


Fear that repairs made at the Pen
dleton and Medford crevasses had suf-
fered heavily from the present rise
were expressed by H. r. Rice of the
levee division of the Arkansas Flood
Commission.


More than 100 900 acres in Chicot
and Desha Counties have been inun-
dated, but less than 200 families have
been affected. All are being cared for
by the Red Cross.

were times today when the market
was actively sold there were other
times when supporting orders were
thrown into the breach in sufficient
quantities to check the decline and
bring about a partial rally.


But the market was a different mar
ket from what it was two weeks ago.
Then hopes were running high in
brokerage circles that Wall Street
was on the verge of another big
speculation for the rise. Day by day
since then these hopes have become
DINNER. Only one set of stocks has
been going up consistently and that
was some of the merger rails. They
have been going up, of course, not
for general reasons, but for reasons
peculiar to themselves.


The market refused to accept their
movement as at all significant of
General conditions and has refused
10 accept their leadership. Wheeling
and Lake Erie doubled its market
price in the last fortnight
without other non-dividendpaying
rails moving more than point and
a half. The merger argument failed
10 take hOld OF the puDIlc magma
ton the way 1t did in the Autumn of
1925.


Gradually this constant failure of
the rushing up Of individual stocks to
exert any influence upon the general
body of the list began to make. senti-
ment uneasy. This uneasiness showed
in the market yesterday and again
today. Prices had quite a break dur
ing the first hour. with the erratic
Wheeling and Lake Erie moving over
a range of five points.

one for recent speciality favorites. 1t

Solvents 'B" and Warner Bros Pic
lures.

weakness threatened to spread and

end Of the forenoon. This, being due

The minute he stepped from the boat
to the pier she was beside him.


The next minute she was in his
arms. Her head was tipped back. In
little patch Of sunlight that came
through the walls of the old pier. he
could see her lovely young face close
to his.


His arms drew her close. held her
tightly against him. His lips found
her own. For a long minute they
clung together. utterly oblivious of
the crowds surging around them. And
Martin Lee realized that at last he
had come into his own.


AS they made their way to the
shining sunlit street beyond, Nan had
forgotten Alicia, and Martin had not
seen her.


Alicia had seen them, however. She
had seen Nan fly into Martins arms
and cling about his neck. She had
seen the look in Martins eyes as he
had gathered her close.


Alicia's corn-fower blue eyes had
grown icy, her lips had drawn into a
straight line as she had quickly
wheeled about so as not to be seem
But she needn't have worried. Neither
OF them could have seen any one else
in that moment of revelation when
they had Clung together. And there
was Summertime ahead of them in
gray, shingled cottage by the sea.


THE END.

deep, swirled on toward the Atlantic
seaboard today, while another of
Winters .barrages crept down the
eastern slopes of the Rockies.

area between the two storms, but low
temperatures spread with the snow
from Canada to the gulf and the
Weather Bureau would promise no
great rise before Sunday, If then.

for Midwestern and Southwestern
States, where a record fall for the
Winter in many places already had
seriously interfered with travel and
communication.


Snow 90 Inches Deep.


Central Illinois was buried deep,
with close to 20 inches of snow on the
ground in some localities, and in
Chicago an army of 5000 labored all
night to keep traffic lanes open.
Three men were killed while attempt
ing TO keep traffic moving and two
others died of exposure


AT Gary, Ind. a street car careened
from snow-hidden rails and crashed
into bus, severely injuring several
persons, and in Chicago the weight of
the snow caved a garage roof in and
hurt four men.

The Southwest shfvered In the I'm.
seasonable weather and prepared for
zero temperatures in the wake of
storming that left snow from an inch
to six inches deep. Virtually all of
Kansas, northern Oklahoma and
Missouri were blanketed with con.
siderable depths.

promised the Middle West today. and
snow-laden skies and low if not ex
treme temperatures were forecast
through the Central States. The storm
center itself swept down the St. Law.
renee Valley to give the corn belt a
breathing spell before the arrival of
the new disturbance advancing east
ward from the Pacific Coast.

AXE VILLA, ILL.,, September IA
R.-Most people would natu-


rally believe that the heavy
IL weight champion of the world,


of all people, is best able to take
care of himself, but not the citizens
of Chicago.


For the first time since Tunny came
West 10 days ago to complete training
for the most expensive fistic display in
history-his $4,000, 900 title battle with
Jack Dempsey at Soldier Field-the
champion today had no one minding
him.


Gene left his personal bodyguard,
Bill Smith of detective headquarters,
spinning yarns of the stock yards and
the bold Chicago gunmen when he de-
parted the training camp Monday to
visit with friends at Lake Forest, 20
miles away.


The situation had not changed
today, for Gene still was visiting and
the sergeant still was spinning his
yarns.


Guards Have Nothing to Do.


And Bill was not the only member
of Genes protective forces left hold
ing the bag" A miniature fire de-
partment, assigned from headquarters
in Chicago, as well as Sergt. Smiths
three assistants. the regular police
force about the grounds, and Jiggs II,
the guarding Marine mascot from
Virginia, all were left with nothing to
protect.


The situation was complicated by
slight peevishness that has crept into
Jiggs' disposition in the past two days.
The husky young bulldog, who cele-
brates his second birthday September
%. the night Gene fights Dempsey,
misses his original master, who gave
him to the Marines last Winter, to re-
place the original Jiggs, a victim of
too many delicacies.


The squad of 20 firemen, detailed
solely for Tunney's protection, has
been slightly handicapped by the non-
appearance of their hose lines. Life
also has become rather vapid for the
score of policemen who guard every
approach to the camp to ward off all
persons without definite business with
in the grounds.


Three More Boxing Days.


With the champion absent, not even
people with business on the grounds
are appearing at the camp. Gene
was due at the country club tonight
for dinner after his three-day absence.
Satisfied that his condition is such that
only three more workouts will fit him
perfectly for the 10round title defense,
Gene will box Thursday and Friday
and probably Sunday before putting
aside his training togs.


Weighing 1872 pounds or thereabouts,
Tunney, according to the consensus of
newspaper critics, is faster than when
he whipped Dempsey last Fall,
stronger, and is boxing and punching
better than at any time in his career.
The added weight. some of which
Gene intends to remove before the
battle, has crept into the punching
equipment about his back and shout
ders. The champion is noticeably
simmer through the waist and hips.


Tunney may visit Tex Rickard. pro-
moter of the show, In Chicago today
before returning to camp. A slight
difference of opinion exists between
the promoter and the champion on the
ticket question. Like some others.
Gene ordered 500 tickets to the big
show and received only 200.

pounds, and had dropped one end on
the trucks standing on the track.

car suspended snapped, allowing the

from the tracks, but the three men
directing the work were directly
under the suspended end Of the car
and were unable to escape, trainmen

FREDERICK, Md, July 25.-Mem-

base ball teams were arrested for play
ing in the local park. The Municipal
swimming pool was thrown open to
the public without charge when base
ball fans threatened action against the
city for charging on Sunday. and the
Barbara Fritchie museum was ordered
closed for the same reason.

Ministerial Association, Lords Day
Alliance and Law and Order League,
demanded the arrest Of the base ball
teams. The base ball officials threat
ened prosecution of the city officials,
and officials of the museum would be
sought if admission charges were
made on Sunday.

leased in $25 bond each. The game
was completed, however. following the
arrests, which were made at the end
of the third inning. Boos greeted the
appearance of the sheriff, and the
more than 1000 fans present con-
tinued to cry play ball." Samuel
Rosenstock. director of the local club,
furnished bond for the players, UNI
pires and gate employees.


HAGERSTOWN, Md. July 25.-
President Augustus Ludwig of the
Hagerstown Base Ball Club. an
nounced today that he would stage a
game here next Sunday between the
Hagerstown and Martinsburg clubs.
The arrests at Frederick yesterday
were made under an ancient State
blue law, which prohibits the staging
of athletic events on Sunday, where
admission is charged.

BY Cable to The Star and Chicago Daily

LONDON, July 23.--The eleventh
hour decision to have the Prince of
Wales, Prince George and Premier
Stanley Baldwin meet Vice President
Dawes at the Buffalo Peace Bridge
was a clever political move by the
pro American section of the British
. cabinet. Chamberlain and Baldwin
and a few other members of the cabi-
net. who are not altogether sympa-
thetic with die hard" methods, have
been striving for months toward a
policy of closer cooperation and bet.
ter understanding with the United
States.


They have frequently been handi-
capped by their colleagues or promi.
nent English people who mistrust the
United States and resent it's prosper
ity. Yet in the last few months the
action of the American destroyers at
Marking and the visit of Lindbergh
have swung English public opinion
toward the Chamberlain viewpoint in
spite of the efforts of the lingo press
to prevent such orientation of public
sentiment.


Orchards Attack America.


The naval disarmament conference
gave the anti-American faction ground
Tor bitter attacks against the
screaming eagle" and in the last few
weeks the patient work of Chamber
lain risked being destroyed.


The die-hards outmaneuvered him
throughout the Geneva discussions,
and the entire press. representing the
United States as bidding for sea SUI
premacy just as Germany did in
1914 succeeded in filling public opin-
ion with resentment and suspicion
against America. Bitter attacks
against the United States can be read
daily in some London journals, and it
is feared such articles. together with
the unsatisfactory developments at
Geneva, might estrange altogether
American public opinion.


Plan Friendly Gesture.


In order to avoid this the King and
Baldwin decided the Prince of Wales
should meet Dawes early in August.
The premier, who will be able to have
a heart-to-heart talk with Secretary of
State Kellogg, has implicit faith in the
Princes popularity in the United
States, and hopes this friendly ges-
ture will help dispel some of the bad
impressions caused lately by venomous
attacks in some papers.

New York city and vicinity escaped
the full fury of the seventy-mile
gale which swept from the North.
western States over the Great Lakes
to the Eastern seacoaSt last night
and early today. western New York
State and the New England seacoast
were hard hit. Bitter cold accom-.
panied the gale. and the mercury
dropped 35 degrees here.

boats were torn from their moor
ings. buildings wrecked and scores

caused by the storm. Squatters on

was accompanied by q blizzard. The
Niagara river rose 10 feet, sub
merged Gamers Island and caused
damage along the river front.

British Columbia. after being marooned

disabled when she struck Vchnefski

BERLIN, September 2.-Potsdam,
home of Prussian glory and militarism
aptly symbolized all Germany last
night. when, under the eye of "neu-
trail" police, republicans, reactionaries
and Communists assembled in the
chief square before the former town
palace of the Hohenzollerns and tried
to shout each other down.


The preteXt was a manifestation
called by the republican Reichs ban
ner organization to protest against
Mayor Rauscher of Potsdam bringing
suit against the Prussian govern
ment for compelling the Potsdam mu-
nicipality to fly the republican tricolor
on constitution day.


Acting according to order, the Pots
dam feactionaries. under the leader
ship of the Steel Helmet Boys, occu-
pied the square, and, reinforced by
about 1000 Communists, blocked the
entrance. When the Reichs banner
procession arrived they found the
square occupied and had to push
through hostile throngs. Despite the
assistance of couple of military
bands, they were unable to make their
speakers heard above the roar of
Kisses, cat calls, whistles and patriotic
hymns sung by the reactionaries.


The police intervened only to pre-
vent fights, and the general demon
stration ended with negative victory
for the reactionaries, who succeeded
in destroying the efforts of the Reichs
banner demonstration, thus summing
up the general condition of political
Germany.

The remains Of Russell Scott, who
hanged himself in the Cook county
jail Saturday night after he had
been reprieved eight times near
the hour of his execution, came
home today-alone.


Just as he mysteriously disap-
peared, hatless and unnoticed, from
his magnificent bridge promotion
offices here five years ago, his body,
now enclosed in a crude pine box,
drew scant attention when it was
trundled onto baggage truck at
the Michigan Central station.


Through the neglect of the train
conductor, the two who kept faith
in Scott during his three year fight
against the moose, were not pres
ent.

Russell's wife, Catherine, whose
heoric efforts were principally re.
sponsible for saving Scott from
death eight times, arrived at the
station 10 minutes later on another
train.

The history of India is far more obscure
than that of China. The Hindus loved poetry
more than history, and before Buddha We have
hardly anything but legend. The Rig-Veda is
a vast collection of folklore dating from 1400

derivatives belongs.


That process of the north sweeping down
with irresistible violence upon the settled and
easy-going south has been the main stream of
history. which each civilization has risen
and fallen like epochal undulations. The Mon
gols poured down upon Peking, the Aryans
upon the Dravidians, the Achaeans and Dorians
upon the Cretans and Aegeans the Latins upon
the aborigines of Italy. the Romans upon the
Cartha ginlans, the Germans upon the Romans
the Lombards upon the Italians the French
upon the Spanish, the English upon the world
Forever the north produces warriors and the
south produces saints. and the weak inherit
Heaven.


So the conquered natives retreated into the

peace. There was little slavery in the viii

caste. The white-skinned handsome conquerors

million words; they who had put together the
Upanishads Tor secret conferences in which

STOMACH GAS, indigestion, gas
Obloating, and other forms of
stomach and bowel trouble are
often due to just one cause-Intes-
tinal Stasis. This increasingly
common disease, which is usually
caused by improper food, lack of
exercise, and other faults of mod
ern life, is said to afflict three
people out of every four.


Intestinal Stasis simply means
the too slow movement of waste
food matter through the intestines.
Instead of being promptly passed
out Of the bowels, this waste mat
ter remains many hours or even
days longer than it should. It
then ferments, forms gas and poi
sons, and causes gas bloating, sour
stomach, indigestion and sleepless.
ness.


A person may have Intestinal
Stasis and yet not be noticeably
constipated. The bowels may move
daily, but the movements are only
partial. Enough old matter is left
to form gas, hinder digestion ane
poison the system.

The two diagrams shown above,
formations for out-of- bounds plays
under PENIS basket. tell an tmpoF-
tant basket ball story. From 1908
through 1915 when a Penn team
lost the ball out-of bounds under
their basket on attack, like every
team in the country. they would
deploy themselves so that every
man covered an opponent. Before
the season of 1916. PENIS coach,
Lon Jourdet, arranged practice
game with a Philadelphia profess
sional outfit, one of its stars being
the late Joe Fogarty, later Yales
basket ball coach. The pros ran
wild against the Quakers. Jourdet
became disguised. Time was called.
His men were "all in" The sug-
gestion was made that Penn prac-
tice defense thereafter. Without
realizing what he was doing, Jour
Diet strung his men out across the
court in Il single file about the
middle. From that moment on the
pros were stopped. Jourdet real
lied he had hit on something. That
season Penn used the new Ave-
man defense in its league games
and emerged with the title. Against
Princeton the defense shown in the
lower panel was used on an out-of-
bounds play.


This was the first use of the Ave-
man defense in basket ball, the
style of defense that is universally
practiced today, usually in a two
line formation.

When a fellow has succeeded, gain
ing all the fame he's needed, piling up
the shining rubles till they make q
noble wad, then his thoughts are
always turning with deep pathetic
yearning, to the town that was his
birthplace, to the old familiar sod.
SO at last, in pomp and splendor,
loaded down with legal tender, he
goes back to see the skyline of old
Punktown by the Moat, where he
sprung his childhood capers, peddling
milk and selling papers, shining
shoes and running errands, anything
to get a groat. In old PunktoWn
bands are playing and the orators are
braying, giving welcome to the native
who has scaled the shining heights;
as he makes a speech explaining what
great happiness he's gaining, every
gesture is applauded by the smiling
village wights. There are pretty girls
around him and the wreaths they
bear confound him, being tributes to
his greatness, to his merit and his
speaking sends his aging blood
a-streaking like hot electric current
through the fbers of his frame.
Here's a guerdon for the cleverl
Here's reward for stern endeavor, for
the long and wearing battle that the
winning man must wage; here's a
solace for the trials, for the pains and

Marshal Chang Tso-Lin. head Of the

recently abrogating the commercial
treaty of 1864 between China and
Spain The treaty had expired, and

tain it's extension until new treaty
was arranged failed.

Sunday, declared that Spain consi6.
cred the Chinese action lacking in
friendship and claimed it violated an
agreement with the foreign minister
covering advantages to be granted
Spain pending the conclusion of
treaty.

Somewhere between the deep ST.
beran forests and the vast Monaghan
desert" the Russian government is re-
ported to have created the worlds
tiniest epublc-TannuTuv


'Tannu-Tuva lies in the valley just
north of the Tannu Mountains and
southwest of 1rkutsk, where the
Uriankhai Tor forest dWellerS) have
long roamed in splendid isolation,
seldom seen by any one except few
traders and agents of the Russian
government" says bulletin from the
National Geographic Society.


Reindeer Is Food.


"The Jrriankhai resemble the round
faced slant eyed Mongolians to the
south and east of them, but lack the
aggressiveness of their Oriental neigh
hors. Hidden away in their valley
domain. they exc out a lazy today
existence with their deer herds The
animals are tame and require little
attention. AS a result, the Uriankhai
spends most of his time lounging
about hi tepee. Often as many as
500 deer will be seen around a tribal
camp of 20 to 80 tepees. They Craze
all day and at nightfall not only re-
turn to the camp. but to the tepee of
their individual owners. Only the off
spring has to be given special care
and the women do that.


Deer milk, deer meat and tender
roots are the principal foods of the
Urankhai and for clothing they wear
deer skins. When they go hunting
they use the deer for transportation
and the fieet-footed animal is even
charged with responsibility for Uri-
ankhai intoxicating liquors. Spirits
are crudely distilled from fermented
deer milk.


when the women are not busy
with the herd. they dress hides With
the aid of deer milk and a wooden
comb, they work the skins until they
become as soft and fine as if tanned
by modern methods. The tepees are
usually full of skins ready to he made
into clothing, and other skins for
mats, harness and for trading.


Modern 'flappers' would envy the
Uriankhai Winter dress, when the
tribesmen and women are entirely
clothed in furs. Sable, lynx and roe
deer cover the Uriankhai's body, while
their boots are usually of roe deer or
musk deer. The cone-shaped hats of
the natives are made of black astra.
khan turned inside out and covered
with colored cloth. a leather belt
from which hang a Russian knife and
a Chinese pipe complete the Uriank.
hal outfit. The young girls dress like
the men. but the married women wear
longer and looser garments In the
Summer they don loose-fitting gar
ments of blue cloth acquired from
Chinese traders.


Trade Furs for Luxuries.


Perhaps few nomad tribes move as
little as the Uriankhai. Only twice
year they roll up the bark tepee
covers and seek new camping
grounds. Their wanderings are al
the convenience of their reindeer
! herds In the Summer the valley
| forests become too hot. so the tribes
men seek higher ground.


Unlike most nomad peoples. the
| Uriankhai have no enemies because
| the natural difficulties of their valley
have kept them almost untouched by
| outside influence


In the Autumn, while the women
break camp and move back into the
valley, the men hunt for hides for the
Winter trading season. From the
Russians and Chinese they get tea
| sugar, wheat flour, tobacco. snuff and
| other Injuries. Sometimes a few
weeks of hunting will net enough mar
ten, fox, roe deer. glutton and snow
leopard hides to buy years supply

She and Tom in a darling stateroon

She smiled softly. They were

After q while the woman no

The woman lay on couch. the

around her waist. Now when he
kissed her neck he hid his face

He wanted her so. and he feared
be was going to lose her.


Her Idols


Roen, who was just nine, used
to watch. These two beings
moved in a shadowy. mysterious
charm. They were Dearie and
Bobby dad, her mother and father.
She wondered about them and
worshiped.


One day she came from school.
A big, fat-faced woman opened
the kitchen door and said:
'Shshsh!' Then she stopped
down. her corsets creaking, and
whispered: you have q little
brother"


Roen stood perfectly still while
these words went tinkling like
Christmas bells in her thought.


This was the gladdest OF the
memories. They had the little
brother.


Afterwards Dearie used to lie
on the couch. Her. hands were
white and thin. But she was
awfully proud. And liked 1t when
Bobby-dad hid his face in her
palms, when he said as though
his heart were breaking, "Oh my
dearest, dearest"


Roen held herself very tight

amber shadows about the old
chintz drapes. Her heart grew
large. She loved them both ter

guessed, with the silence and
yearning Of childhood.


Don't Cry"


It was only a small house where
they lived. But they had two won.
drous pictures that an artist
friend had painted. One was
called Morning Light" 1t showed
fishermen putting out to a misty
lavender. There, too, were the
rich old chintzes. And always a
flower in the vase.


! Ever since Jackie was born they
ate here. They pushed the table
to Dearie's couch.


Roen picked nasturtiums on big.

table was set, she would say:
Bring me purple pansies and

hair and look pale and thrilling

waited for the warm, adoring flush
to deepen her fathers eyes. Young
as she was, she felt a radiant
sweetness. There grew, subcon-
sciously in her thought, the dream

One day, when she was thirteen,

fat-faced, came to her. walking
mysteriously. Your father wants
you. Now-whatever you do,

memories cut deep in incompre.
hensible pain.


Her father had been in bed for

Roen had not been allowed to see
him. Once she had stolen to his
door and had been frightened by

breathing.


She followed Maggie reluctantly,
They tiptoed across the living
room where Dearie lay face down.

NEW YORK, February 2i,-The
stock market was thrown into n
turmoil midway through the after
noon today when news came from
Washington that the Supreme Court
had decided the valuation case of the
Los Angeles and Salt Lake Railroad
against the Interstate Commerce Com
mission adversely to the railroads.
This was entirely contrary to the
general expectation in Wall Street,
which had built its hopes on the prece-
dent established in recent decisions by
the court in utility litigation.


The first result was the dumping
overheard of railroad shares, both
dividend paying and low priced, for
anything they would bring. Quotations
melted away. Losses ran up to 8
points and more before support was
encountered. The heaviest sufferers
were those roads with a large cap
italiZation in proportion property
value The Kansas City So .ern and
the st. Louis-San Francisco are the
classic examples of carriers in this
position.


The recent excessive speculation in
low-priced so-called merger shares was
largely undone in a very short time.
This selling carried down with it
railroad stocks about the value of
which there is no doubt, such as the
Atchison, the NorfC and Western
and others in that group. Probably
the majority of the high-grade divi-
dendpaying roads have property
value more than sufficient to support
their present prices, but in the con-
fusion of the hour all this was for
gotten.


After the first flood of selling there
came a rally which recovered good
deal of the earlier loss in some in
stances.


Rock Island, for example, a road
with large property value, but low
earning power, came back quickly.
Some of the Northwestern roads met
equally good support and even Kan
sas City Southern recovered from it's
low. But before this had happened
a good many spectators with thin
margins had been eliminated from the
picture.


The selling in the rails spread to
the industrials when it was at it's
height. General Motors came down
and SO did Allied Chemical, which had
been so strong earlier in the session.
Baldwin, too, lost large part of the
morning rally of seven points.


Before news of the Supreme Court
decision had been received the mar
ket had been generally firm. with here
Nnd there some sharp advances.
